text: In the IRLS step-halving loop, `edi_check_R_user_interrupt_every(s)` is called with s = 0 on the first probe of every outer iteration. Because 0 % 16 == 0, every IRLS iteration runs `Rcpp::checkUserInterrupt()` (R_ToplevelExec) and `edi_check_time_budget()`, which evaluates the R call `proc.time()` through `Rcpp::Function`. That is a full R evaluation with a tryCatch wrapper and a result allocation, costing several microseconds each time. The outer loop already calls `edi_check_R_user_interrupt_every(iter)` with the usual stride of 16. The halving loop runs at most 10 O(n) probes, so it does not need its own check. Removing it brings the interrupt and time-budget polling back to the intended stride. For typical Poisson fits (n of a few hundred to a few thousand, small p), an IRLS iteration costs only tens of microseconds of exp and crossprod work, so the per-iteration R round-trip is a noticeable fraction of the fit.

applied_text: // Fused, allocation-free weight update (same per-element arithmetic
text: Each IRLS iteration builds the Huber or bisquare weights through materialized Eigen arrays: `u`, `abs_u` and, for MM, `tmp`. That is 2-3 heap allocations of length n, plus as many extra full passes over memory, before the result is written into res.w. This change replaces them with one scalar loop that reads r and writes res.w in place. It does the same arithmetic per element in the same order: u = r_i/scale, |u|, then for MM t = 1 - (u/c_b)*(u/c_b), w = t*t; for M, w = c/|u|. This removes the per-iteration mallocs and frees and roughly 2-3 of the ~20-25 length-n memory passes per iteration when p is small (as in the bootstrap path, p = 2 + p_cov). Scale is read into a local so the stores to w do not force it to be reloaded.
